title: Chicken Chettinad
description: Chicken simmered in a coarse, freshly roasted masala of coriander, fennel, star anise and dried red chillies — genuinely spicy-hot from the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu, not just heavily spiced, with a deep roasted aroma.

ingredients.note: reduce to 2 for a milder batch

steps: Dry roast the coriander seeds, dried red chillies, cumin, fennel, peppercorns, cinnamon, cloves and star anise in a pan over low heat for 2-3 minutes until fragrant and slightly darkened.
Add the grated coconut to the same pan and roast a further 1-2 minutes until it turns light golden, then cool and grind everything to a coarse paste with a splash of water.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan, add the curry leaves and onion, and cook over medium heat until the onion turns golden.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and saute for a minute until the raw smell disappears.
Add the chicken and sear on medium-high heat for 4-5 minutes until it changes colour on all sides.
Lower the heat, add the ground masala paste and turmeric, and cook, stirring often, for 5-6 minutes until the oil starts to separate — this roasted masala catches easily, so keep the heat low.
Add the tomato and salt, cover and simmer for 15-18 minutes until the chicken is tender.
Uncover and simmer a few minutes more to thicken the gravy to a coating consistency, then finish with coriander leaves.
tips: Roast the whole spices and coconut low and slow — pushed too far they turn bitter instead of nutty.
Cook the ground masala on low heat until the oil visibly separates; that's the sign the raw spice taste is gone.
kidNote: Halve the dried red chillies (or drop to two) in the batch you'll serve the kids and skip any extra pepper, then finish their bowls with a spoonful of coconut milk or yogurt stirred through — the roasted coriander, fennel and cinnamon still carry the Chettinad flavour without the heat.
nutritionNote: A good source of lean protein from the chicken; the roasted-spice masala uses less added fat than a cream-based curry, so it pairs well with plain rice without tipping the meal too rich.

title: Rogan Josh
description: Bone-in mutton or beef braised low and slow in whisked yogurt with fennel, dry ginger powder and Kashmiri chilli for its signature deep red colour — no onion or garlic, warmly spiced rather than fiery, with a rich, clingy gravy.

ingredients.item: bone-in mutton or beef stew pieces

steps: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy pot until it just starts to smoke, then let it cool for a minute to lose its raw sharpness.
Add the bay leaf, black cardamom, green cardamom, cloves and cinnamon, and let them sizzle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the meat and sear on high heat, turning occasionally, for 8-10 minutes until browned on all sides.
Lower the heat and stir in the asafoetida and Kashmiri chilli powder with a splash of water so the powder blooms without scorching.
Add the whisked yogurt a spoonful at a time, stirring constantly over low heat so it doesn't split, until it's fully incorporated.
Stir in the fennel powder, dry ginger powder and salt.
Add the water, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low heat for 45-60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the meat is fork-tender and the gravy has thickened.
Uncover and simmer a few minutes more if the gravy needs reducing, then serve hot.
tips: Add the yogurt off direct high heat and stir constantly — this is the step that prevents the gravy from curdling.
Letting the smoking mustard oil cool slightly before the spices go in keeps its pungency from turning bitter.
kidNote: Use the lower end of the Kashmiri chilli powder (or halve it) for the portion you'll serve the kids — it's a mild variety used mostly for colour, but a lighter hand keeps their share properly gentle — and stir a spoonful of extra yogurt through their gravy. The whole spices stay in for aroma without any real heat.
nutritionNote: A protein- and iron-rich meat braise; the gravy relies on yogurt rather than cream for body, which keeps the saturated fat lower than a butter-based curry — pair with rice or roti and a green vegetable side.

title: Rava Dosa
description: A thin, lacy, instant semolina crepe with no fermentation needed — crisp at the edges, studded with cumin and curry leaves, South India's quick-fix breakfast dosa served with coconut chutney and sambar.
steps: Whisk the semolina, rice flour, maida and salt together in a large bowl.
Add the water gradually, whisking out any lumps, until the batter is thin and watery — much runnier than a regular dosa batter.
Rest the batter for 20-30 minutes so the semolina fully absorbs the water, then stir well again before cooking.
Stir in the cumin seeds, crushed pepper, ginger, green chilli, curry leaves, coriander leaves and onion if using.
Heat a flat dosa tawa or nonstick pan over medium-high heat until a drop of batter sizzles on contact.
Stir the batter again, then pour it from a height in a circular motion from the outer edge inward, leaving natural lacy gaps — do not spread it with a ladle like a regular dosa.
Drizzle a little oil around the edges and cook until the dosa turns golden and crisp and lifts easily off the pan, 2-3 minutes.
Fold into a half-moon or quarter and serve immediately with coconut chutney and sambar; repeat with the remaining batter, stirring it each time since the flours settle.
tips: A thin, watery batter is what gives rava dosa its lacy holes — thick batter turns it into a pancake instead.
Cook these one at a time straight from the heat; unlike regular dosa, rava dosa doesn't hold well once made ahead.
nutritionNote: Lighter than a rice-and-lentil dosa since it skips fermentation, though it's still a refined-carbohydrate breakfast — round it out with a vegetable-forward sambar or coconut chutney rather than a second fried side.

title: Upma
description: Roasted semolina tempered with mustard seeds, lentils, cashews and curry leaves, then cooked soft and fluffy in hot water — a mild, quick South Indian breakfast that's on the table in under 20 minutes of actual cooking.
steps: Dry roast the semolina in a wide pan over low-medium heat for 4-5 minutes, stirring constantly, until it smells nutty but stays pale; set aside.
In the same pan, heat the ghee and add the mustard seeds; once they splutter, add the urad dal, chana dal and cashews and fry until golden.
Add the curry leaves, green chilli and ginger, and saute for 30 seconds.
Add the onion and cook until translucent.
Add the water and salt, and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and slowly stream in the roasted semolina with one hand while stirring continuously with the other to prevent lumps.
Cover and cook on low heat for 2-3 minutes until all the water is absorbed and the semolina is soft and fluffy.
Fluff with a fork, drizzle over the lemon juice, and garnish with coriander leaves before serving.
tips: Streaming the rava in slowly while stirring is the only way to avoid lumps — dumping it in all at once guarantees them.
Roast the semolina just until fragrant; over-roasted rava turns the finished upma dry and grainy.
nutritionNote: A light, quickly digested breakfast; the lentils and cashews add a little protein and the onion some fibre, but it's low in vegetables overall, so pair with fruit or a side of yogurt to round out the meal.

title: Matar Paneer
description: Paneer cubes and green peas simmered in a dhaba-style onion-tomato gravy built from separately fried onions and boiled tomatoes — mildly warm, quick weeknight comfort food without any cream or cashews.
steps: Boil the tomato in a little water for 5-6 minutes until soft, then cool and blend to a smooth puree.
Shallow-fry the onion in a tablespoon of the oil until deep golden, then cool and grind to a smooth paste.
Heat the remaining oil in a pan and add the cumin seeds and bay leaf; let them sizzle until fragrant.
Add the onion paste and cook over medium heat, stirring, for 3-4 minutes until the oil separates.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and saute for a minute until the raw smell disappears.
Lower the heat and stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and coriander powder with a splash of water so the powders bloom without catching.
Add the tomato puree and cook, stirring often, for 7-8 minutes until it thickens and the oil separates again.
Add enough water to loosen the gravy, then add the peas and simmer 6-8 minutes until tender.
Add the paneer, garam masala, kasuri methi and salt; simmer 2-3 minutes just to warm the paneer through, then finish with coriander leaves.
tips: Grinding the fried onion and boiled tomato separately, instead of cooking them together raw, is what gives this gravy its dhaba-style depth.
Add the paneer right at the end and don't let it boil hard, or it turns rubbery.
nutritionNote: Paneer and peas together bring protein, calcium and fibre, and this version skips cream entirely, keeping the fat mostly to the tempering oil — a good vegetarian main to pair with a lighter dal-and-rice night.

title: Baingan Bharta
description: A whole eggplant charred over an open flame until the skin blisters and the flesh turns smoky-soft, then mashed and cooked down with onion, tomato and ginger — properly spicy-hot, letting the char come through rather than burying it in cream.
steps: Pierce the eggplant a few times with a knife, rub lightly with oil, and roast it directly over an open gas flame (or under a hot grill), turning occasionally, for 12-15 minutes until the skin is blackened and blistered all over and a knife slides through the flesh easily.
Let the eggplant cool, then peel off the charred skin under running water and discard the stem; roughly mash the smoky flesh with a fork.
Heat the oil in a pan and add the cumin seeds; let them sizzle until fragrant.
Add the onion and cook over medium heat until golden brown.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and green chilli, and saute for a minute.
Add the tomato and cook, stirring often, until it softens and turns pulpy.
Lower the heat and stir in the turmeric and chilli powder with a splash of water so they bloom without scorching.
Add the mashed eggplant and salt, and cook uncovered over medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring often, until the mixture dries out and no longer tastes raw.
Sprinkle over the garam masala, mix, and finish with coriander leaves.
tips: Charring the eggplant directly over a flame is what makes bharta taste smoky — an oven-roasted eggplant cooks through but misses that flavour, so finish it briefly under the broiler if that's your only option.
Cook the mashed eggplant uncovered until it visibly dries and thickens; a wet bharta tastes unfinished.
kidNote: Skip the green chilli and use half the red chilli powder in the batch for the kids, and stir their portion in a minute earlier so it spends less time over direct heat — the smoky char and cumin-onion base still carry the dish without the sharp heat.
nutritionNote: Eggplant is naturally low in calories and a decent source of fibre; this version uses no cream, so it's one of the lighter vegetable sides here — good to pair with a protein-rich dal or rajma.

title: Beans Poriyal
description: Finely chopped green beans stir-fried with a mustard-seed and urad dal tempering, then tossed with fresh grated coconut — a dry, mild South Indian vegetable side that keeps its crunch and bright colour.
steps: Heat the coconut oil in a wide pan and add the mustard seeds; let them splutter.
Add the urad dal, dried red chillies and curry leaves, and fry until the dal turns golden.
Add the chopped beans, turmeric and salt, and toss well to coat in the tempering.
Add a splash of water, cover, and cook over low-medium heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are just tender but still bright green.
Uncover and cook a minute longer over higher heat to evaporate any remaining moisture, so the poriyal stays dry rather than steamed.
Stir in the grated coconut, toss for a minute to warm it through, and serve.
tips: Chop the beans small and even so they cook through in the same time without turning mushy.
Add the coconut right at the end off the heat if serving later — it stays freshest that way.
nutritionNote: A fibre- and vitamin-rich vegetable side that's naturally low in fat; the coconut is used sparingly as a finish rather than a sauce, so it pairs well even on days you're serving a richer curry.

title: Lemon Rice
description: Cooled cooked rice tossed through a crackling mustard-seed, peanut and curry-leaf tempering with a generous squeeze of lemon — a mildly tangy South Indian rice dish that travels well in a lunchbox.
steps: Cook the rice ahead of time and spread it out to cool completely, fluffing the grains apart so they stay separate rather than clumping.
Heat the oil in a pan and fry the peanuts until crunchy; remove and set aside.
In the same oil, add the mustard seeds; once they splutter, add the urad dal and chana dal and fry until golden.
Add the dried red chilli, green chilli, curry leaves and asafoetida, and fry for a few seconds.
Add the turmeric powder and stir through.
Add the cooled rice and salt, and toss gently with a wide spatula to coat evenly without mashing the grains.
Take the pan off the heat, squeeze in the lemon juice, and toss again, tasting and adjusting salt or lemon as needed.
Garnish with the roasted peanuts and coriander leaves before serving.
tips: Day-old, fully cooled rice works best — warm rice turns gummy the moment the lemon juice hits it.
Add the lemon juice off the heat; direct heat mutes its fresh tang.
nutritionNote: A light carbohydrate base with a modest lift of protein and healthy fat from the peanuts; it's a plain rice dish on its own, so serve alongside a dal, poriyal or curry rather than as the whole meal.

title: Prawn Masala
description: Prawns simmered in a ground coconut-and-whole-spice masala with onion and tomato — a coastal Konkan-style curry, tangy and properly spicy-hot, distinct from a coconut-milk fish curry since the coconut here is ground into the base, not poured in.

ingredients.note: reduce to 2 for a milder batch

steps: Toss the prawns with turmeric, salt and lemon juice, and set aside to marinate for 15 minutes.

Dry roast the coriander seeds, dried red chillies, cumin, fennel, cinnamon and cloves in a pan for 1-2 minutes until fragrant, then cool and grind with the grated coconut and a little water to a smooth paste.
Heat the oil in a pan and add the curry leaves and onion; cook over medium heat until golden.
Add the ginger-garlic paste and saute for a minute until the raw smell disappears.
Add the ground coconut masala paste and cook, stirring often, over low heat for 5-6 minutes until the oil starts to separate.
Add the tomato and cook until it softens and breaks down.
Add enough water to bring the gravy to a curry consistency, bring to a simmer, and cook 5 minutes for the flavours to meld.
Slide in the marinated prawns and cook for 4-5 minutes, just until they turn pink and curl — do not overcook or they turn rubbery.
Sprinkle over the garam masala and finish with coriander leaves.
tips: Prawns cook fast — pull them off the heat the moment they curl into a tight 'C' shape, or they turn tough.
Roasting the whole spices before grinding is what separates this from a plain coconut-milk curry; don't skip it.
kidNote: The ground dried-chilli masala makes this a proper spicy-hot curry rather than a mild one, so it isn't a safe one to serve straight to the kids. Set aside a few plain-poached prawns (simmered separately in a little of the tomato-onion base with just turmeric and salt) and spoon a little of that milder gravy over their rice instead.
nutritionNote: Prawns are a lean, high-protein seafood option; ground coconut adds some saturated fat but far less than a coconut-milk-based curry, so this pairs well with plain rice and a vegetable side.

title: Sooji Halwa
description: Semolina roasted in ghee until fragrant, then bloomed with warm sugar syrup and cardamom until glossy and soft — a quick, saffron-tinted festival sweet studded with fried cashews and raisins.
steps: Heat 2 tablespoons of the ghee in a pan and fry the cashews and raisins until the cashews turn golden and the raisins plump up; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining ghee to the same pan and add the semolina; roast over low-medium heat, stirring constantly, for 8-10 minutes until fragrant and lightly golden — do not let it brown.
Meanwhile, warm the water with the sugar and saffron in a separate pot, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Slowly pour the warm sugar water into the roasted semolina while stirring continuously with the other hand — it will bubble and splutter, so add it carefully in a thin stream.
Stir in the cardamom powder, then cover and cook on low heat for 2-3 minutes until all the liquid is absorbed and the semolina turns soft and glossy.
Fold in the fried cashews and raisins, and finish with an extra drizzle of ghee before serving warm.
tips: Pour the liquid in slowly and keep stirring — dumping it in fast causes hard lumps that never soften.
Roast the semolina only until fragrant and pale gold; over-roasting makes the finished halwa taste dry and dense.
nutritionNote: A ghee- and sugar-rich sweet best kept to an occasional treat rather than a daily dessert; the cashews add a little protein and healthy fat, but portion it small alongside a lighter main meal.
